title: Gold leaf cake decoration
subtitle: applying edible gold leaf to buttercream, fondant, and chocolate
excerpt: Edible gold leaf adds metallic sheen to celebration cakes and truffles. The leaf is extremely fragile and sticks to any slightly tacky surface, including buttercream and slightly-set ganache. The key skill is transferring it without it crumpling: a dry brush and a calm, unhurried approach make the difference.
sourceNotes: Edible gold leaf application technique used in professional pâtisserie; leaf-on-cake decoration widely documented in UK and European cake-decorating instruction from the 2000s onward.

glossaryTerms.definition: Ultra-thin sheets of pure gold (24 carat or alloyed down) that are safe to eat and used in professional confectionery for decorative metallic effect.

content.text: is sold in booklets of 8 to 10 cm square sheets, interleaved with tissue. It adheres to any tacky surface by static attraction, which means you never touch it with your fingers and never breathe directly onto it. The leaf is thinner than a soap bubble and will tear or crumple instantly if handled incorrectly.

Gold leaf sticks to buttercream that is at room temperature (not fridge-cold and not oily), to ganache within the first hour after pouring, and to fondant lightly brushed with a tiny amount of clear alcohol (vodka) or cooled boiled water. A completely dry or set surface will not hold it.
Work in a draught-free space. Turn off any fans, close windows, and avoid speaking near the leaf while transferring it. Gold leaf moves with the slightest air current.
Open the booklet and fold back the tissue to expose one sheet of leaf. Do not remove the leaf from the booklet yet.

Bring the open booklet close to the cake surface. Use a dry, clean artist's brush or gilding brush to gently push a corner of the leaf onto the tacky surface. The leaf will transfer as the brush touches it.
Lay the rest of the sheet flat by lowering the booklet and letting the leaf settle. Do not stretch or drag it; let it settle naturally.
Use the tip of the dry brush to press and smooth the leaf gently onto the surface, working from the centre out. Any tears or overlapping fragments can be dabbed into gaps with the brush tip.
For a broken or patchy look, tear pieces from the sheet and apply individually. There is no single correct approach; apply more or fewer pieces depending on the effect you want.

attrs.problem: Leaf crumpling on contact with the cake
attrs.avoid: Avoid placing the leaf too far above the surface; the transfer distance should be very short.
attrs.fix: Bring the booklet to within 1 cm of the surface before touching the corner with the brush.

attrs.problem: Leaf not sticking to the surface
attrs.avoid: Avoid applying to a cold, firm surface; the leaf needs a slightly soft or tacky substrate.
attrs.fix: For fondant, brush the area with a tiny amount of cooled boiled water and wait 30 seconds for it to become tacky before applying.
